screens.title: Capstone: Smart Home Environment Station
screens.subtitle: A practical project that brings sensors, logging, MQTT, and a web dashboard together

narration.text: Welcome. In this capstone brief you will see a clear, project-focused plan for a smart home environment station that runs on a Raspberry Pi. The goal is not only to read sensors, but to make those readings useful: show them on a small display, store them in a CSV file for analysis, publish them to MQTT topics so other devices can subscribe, and expose them on a simple Flask web page. You will also learn how to trigger an alert when a temperature threshold is exceeded and how to ensure the monitoring script starts automatically at boot using a systemd service or cron job. A concrete example is measuring temperature and humidity every five seconds and light every ten seconds, then publishing values to topics like home/temperature and home/humidity while appending a timestamped row to a CSV. As you work, keep documentation and a wiring diagram so others can reproduce your setup. By the end, you should understand the end-to-end structure and what to demonstrate for assessment, and be ready to customize enclosure, sampling intervals, or alert logic to match your environment.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after completing this capstone

narration.text: By the end of this capstone you will be able to assemble sensors and displays on a Raspberry Pi, configure a monitoring script to sample sensors at specific intervals, and produce reliable logged and networked data. First, you will test each sensor individually so you can confirm readings before integrating them. For example, reading a DHT22 value in the terminal helps isolate wiring errors early. Second, you will format and display the latest readings on an I2C display so local users can see values immediately. Third, you will implement CSV logging that appends timestamped rows to a file; that ensures you have a persistent record to analyze. Finally for this screen, you will publish readings to MQTT topics to enable remote subscribers or automation. Each objective focuses on a practical competency that will be assessed: readable sensors, stable display updates, a growing CSV log, and working MQTT messages. Keep in mind a common misconception: testing a sensor in isolation is not optional—it prevents wasting time integrating faulty wiring. As you practice, ask yourself which step you can verify quickly so you can progress confidently.

First, you will implement alert logic: configure a user-defined temperature threshold and activate an LED or small fan when exceeded. This behavior gives an immediate, physical indication when conditions require attention. Second, you will ensure the monitoring script starts at boot, using a systemd service or a cron job; systemd is preferred when you want automatic restarts after crashes. screens.title: Project Requirements Explained
screens.subtitle: A precise definition of functional requirements and why each matters

narration.text: Let's define the functional requirements for the environment station so you know what success looks like. The brief lists discrete responsibilities: periodic reads of temperature and humidity every five seconds and light every ten seconds, a display showing the latest values, a CSV log with timestamps, MQTT publishing of temperature and humidity to topics such as home/temperature and home/humidity, a Flask web page showing latest values, an alert LED triggered above a configured threshold, an auto-start mechanism using systemd or cron, and full documentation including a wiring diagram. Each requirement solves a real problem: frequent reads provide timely data without flooding resources; a local display gives instant feedback while CSV logs create a persistent record for analysis; MQTT enables other devices or services to subscribe without polling the Pi; and a web dashboard allows networked access from any browser. A common misconception is that frequent sampling must be maximal; in practice you choose intervals that balance timeliness and C P U or network load. For example, sampling temperature every five seconds is responsive for room conditions, while a ten-second light sampling reduces ADC overhead. The takeaway: meeting each requirement ensures the station is useful, networked, and demonstrable for grading.

screens.title: Recommended Milestones
screens.subtitle: Five-day milestone plan to structure development and testing

narration.text: A clear milestone plan helps you progress steadily and test at each stage. The brief recommends a five-day schedule. Day one: set up the Pi, install necessary packages, and test each sensor individually by printing values to the terminal. This helps isolate wiring and library issues. Day two: add the display and format the output so the local screen shows clear labels and stable updates without flicker. Day three: implement CSV logging and MQTT publishing so you have both a persistent file and networked messages. Day four: build the simple Flask dashboard and add the alert logic that turns on an LED or fan when temperature exceeds a threshold. Day five: add auto-start using systemd or cron, assemble the hardware into an enclosure, perform full-system tests, and write the README and wiring diagram. An important practical tip is to verify each milestone with specific checks: a growing CSV file, MQTT messages received by a subscriber, dashboard reachable from another device, and the alert engaging at the configured threshold. Following these milestones reduces integration risk and ensures you can demonstrate working features for assessment.

screens.title: Sensor Reading and CSV Logging
screens.subtitle: Core script structure: read sensors, timestamp, append to CSV

narration.text: This lesson walks through the core loop that reads sensors and writes CSV rows. The essential pattern is: import the sensor library, read the sensor, validate that the reading is not None, get a timestamp, append a row to a CSV file, and optionally publish or update a display. A concrete example in the brief shows reading a DHT22 and appending timestamp and temperature to temperature_log. csv every ten seconds. A common misconception is to assume every library read will succeed; in practice you must check for None or invalid readings and handle retries. Also avoid opening and closing a CSV file inefficiently in a tight loop; open with append each write or buffer writes and flush periodically depending on memory constraints. Another important detail is readable output formatting: format numeric values to a reasonable precision for both the CSV and display. The takeaway is to design a resilient loop that both preserves data in a file and continues operating even if a single sensor read fails, using retries, logging failures, and not crashing the whole process. Sensor Reading and CSV Logging means validate sensor reads, timestamp each row, append to csv safely, and handle failed reads to keep the service running.. In practical terms, core script structure: read sensors, timestamp, append to csv. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Data Flows: Display, Log, Publish, Web
screens.subtitle: How sensor data moves from hardware to users and services

narration.text: Understanding the system architecture clarifies where each piece fits. Sensor readings flow into the main monitoring script running on the Raspberry Pi. The script writes values to a CSV file for local persistence, updates a 16x2 I2C LCD or small OLED for immediate local feedback, publishes temperature and humidity to MQTT topics that other devices can subscribe to, and serves a simple Flask page that shows the latest values to browsers on the network. This multi-output architecture gives redundancy: if the network is down, the CSV still captures data and the local display still shows current values. A common misconception is that one output is enough—relying solely on MQTT or the web dashboard creates single points of failure. For alerts, the architecture includes a GPIO-controlled LED or relay that is actuated when the script detects a threshold breach; this produces an instantaneous physical signal that is independent of network latency. The practical example to test is end-to-end: verify a sensor reading appears on the display, is appended to the CSV, is received by an MQTT subscriber, and is visible on the Flask page. That proves each data flow component is working together.

keyIdea.title: Multi-output Flow
keyIdea.text: Send readings to multiple outputs—display, CSV, MQTT, and web—so the system is resilient to network or single-service failures.

screens.title: Sensor Options and Trade-offs
screens.subtitle: Choosing DHT22 vs DHT11 and analog vs digital light sensors

narration.text: This slide compares the sensor options the brief mentions so you can choose appropriately. The DHT22 and DHT11 are both temperature and humidity sensors commonly used with Raspberry Pi projects. The brief lists either DHT22 or DHT11; choose the DHT22 when you need higher accuracy or a wider humidity range, and choose the DHT11 if you need a lower-cost, simpler sensor. For light measurement, you can use an analog light-dependent resistor with an MCP3008 ADC or a digital light sensor module. The analog LDR plus ADC is flexible and inexpensive but requires extra wiring and conversion via the MCP3008. A digital light sensor module gives a direct digital reading and often simpler code. A common misconception is that all sensors are drop-in replacements. They often require different wiring, libraries, and timing constraints. For example, analog sensors need an ADC and careful mapping of values, while digital sensors may use I2C or a one-wire protocol. Choose based on your priorities: cost and availability, wiring complexity, required precision, and library support on Raspberry Pi OS. The takeaway: pick sensors that match your accuracy needs and the complexity you’re ready to handle.

keyIdea.title: Sensor Trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Select sensors by balancing accuracy, wiring complexity, and library support: DHT22 for accuracy, DHT11 for cost; ADC for analog LDR, or choose a digital light module for simplicity.

screens.title: MQTT Publishing and Topics
screens.subtitle: How to publish readings and what the assessment expects

narration.text: Publishing to MQTT connects your station to other devices and services. The brief requires publishing temperature and humidity to topics such as home/temperature and home/humidity. Implement a small MQTT client in your monitoring script, connect to a broker—often running locally or on the network—and publish each new reading as a simple payload. Use a clear topic naming convention so subscribers can find the data easily. A practical example: publish a numeric temperature string or a compact JSON payload containing both temperature and humidity. The assessment expects messages to be received by a subscriber or command-line tool. A common misconception is to assume that publishing once at startup is enough; instead publish regularly as readings change so subscribers have current data. Also handle broker connection failures gracefully: queue or retry publishes and log failures without crashing the script. Finally, remember to avoid embedding sensitive credentials in public code; document where credentials are stored and how to configure a local broker for testing. The takeaway: reliable, periodic MQTT publishes with sensible topic names and error handling are required for a passing project.

keyIdea.title: MQTT Best Practices
keyIdea.text: Publish periodic readings to clear topics, handle broker failures with retries, and ensure messages are demonstrably received by a subscriber for assessment.

Error handling

Assessment check

Key Takeaway

screens.title: Flask Web Dashboard
screens.subtitle: Minimal server to expose latest readings to the network

narration.text: The brief requires a simple Flask web page that shows the latest values and refreshes automatically or on demand. A straightforward architecture is to have the monitoring script write the latest reading to a small JSON file or an in-memory cache, and let the Flask app read that file or cache when serving the page. Alternatively, the monitoring script and Flask app can be the same long-running process that shares variables. When serving on the network, set the Flask host to 0.0.0.0 so other devices can access the page. The assessment expects the dashboard to be accessible from another device. A misconception is to expose the server without considering access methods; in a classroom or home network, host=0.0.0.0 is fine, but document how to reach the IP address for grading. Keep the page minimal: show timestamp, temperature, humidity, and light, and include a button or auto-refresh meta tag to update values. Also test concurrency: ensure that reading the shared file or cache is safe when the monitoring script writes simultaneously. The takeaway: a simple, reliable Flask endpoint displaying the latest values is sufficient and should be demonstrably reachable from another device.

keyIdea.title: Minimal Dashboard
keyIdea.text: Serve the latest sensor values via a small Flask app reachable on the local network, ensuring safe sharing of the latest reading between the monitor and the web server.

  • Keep the UI minimal: timestamp, temp, humidity, light, and an update control.
Test & demonstrate
From another device, open the Pi's IP address and verify the page shows the latest reading. Document the URL and access steps in your README for grading.
Key Takeaway
A lightweight Flask page with reliable shared data is enough; ensure it is reachable and documented for assessment.

screens.title: Alert Logic and Actuation
screens.subtitle: Implementing a threshold and a physical notification

narration.text: Alert logic connects sensor values to a physical output. The brief requires turning on an alert LED when temperature exceeds a user-defined threshold; optionally a relay and fan can be activated. Implement this by comparing the latest temperature reading to a threshold variable you expose in configuration or the web dashboard. When the reading exceeds the threshold, set the GPIO output high to power the LED or trigger the relay. Ensure you use a current-limiting resistor for LEDs and a suitable relay module for higher-voltage loads. A common mistake is toggling the GPIO rapidly when readings hover near the threshold; use hysteresis or a short debounce window so the alert does not flicker. Also consider safety: do not drive high-current loads directly from GPIO—use a relay or transistor driver. For testing, choose a threshold that you can trigger reliably during demo and show both activation and deactivation. The takeaway: reliable alert behavior requires safe wiring, a debounced threshold, and clear documentation of the pin and trigger condition for grading. Alert Logic and Actuation means trigger alerts with gpio using safe wiring, hysteresis to avoid flicker, and documented thresholds so activation is repeatable for assessment.. In practical terms, implementing a threshold and a physical notification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safe Alerts
keyIdea.text: Trigger alerts with GPIO using safe wiring, hysteresis to avoid flicker, and documented thresholds so activation is repeatable for assessment.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.4 › Alert Logic
Implementation steps
  1. Define a user-set threshold in config or UI.
  2. Compare latest temperature to threshold on each read.
  3. Set GPIO output high when above threshold, low when below with hysteresis.
  4. Use proper current limiting, relay modules, or drivers for safety.
Testing checklist
  • Confirm LED lights at the configured threshold.
  • Verify relay and fan, if used, engage safely.
  • Show hysteresis prevents rapid toggling around the threshold.
Caution
Never drive high-current devices directly from a GPIO pin; use a relay module or transistor driver and document wiring clearly.

screens.title: Auto-start and Service Management
screens.subtitle: Start the monitoring script automatically and keep it running

narration.text: The brief asks for automatic startup so the station runs unattended after power cycles. Two common approaches are a systemd service or a cron @reboot entry. Systemd is preferred because it supports automatic restarts, dependency ordering, and logging. Create a simple service file that describes the user, the working directory, the executable script, and restart behavior. For example, set Restart=on-failure so the service restarts after crashes. Use journalctl -u yourservice to review logs during debugging. A cron @reboot line can work for simple cases, but it lacks restart control. A common misconception is to assume a script in rc. local will provide the same robustness as systemd; it generally will not. Also ensure your service runs with appropriate permissions and does not require an interactive session. Document the service file format, enable it with systemctl enable, and test by rebooting the Pi to ensure the monitoring script starts and continues logging. The final demonstration should show the script running after a reboot and producing CSV rows, MQTT messages, and display updates without manual intervention. Auto-start and Service Management means use systemd for auto-start and automatic restarts, document the service file, and test by rebooting to demonstrate unattended operation.. In practical terms, start the monitoring script automatically and keep it running. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Service Reliability
keyIdea.text: Use systemd for auto-start and automatic restarts, document the service file, and test by rebooting to demonstrate unattended operation.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.4 › Auto-start
Use systemd
Write a service unit with ExecStart pointing to your monitoring script, set Restart=on-failure, enable it with systemctl enable, and check logs with journalctl -u yourservice.
Alternative: cron @reboot
A cron @reboot entry may be acceptable for simple demos but lacks automatic restart and richer logging compared to systemd.
Key Takeaway
Prefer systemd for a robust auto-start solution and document the service file and enable steps for grading.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Three central ideas to keep in mind

narration.text: Let's summarize three essential concepts you will carry forward. First: test sensors individually before integration. This prevents wasted time chasing wiring or library issues once you are assembling multiple components. Second: design a resilient monitoring loop that validates readings, timestamps values, appends to a CSV, and recovers from occasional failures so the service remains running. Third: provide multiple outputs—local display for immediate feedback, CSV for persistence, MQTT for networked access, and a small Flask page for browser viewing—so your project is usable and demonstrable in different scenarios. Each concept connects to the assessment; demonstrating them clearly will help you achieve a passing grade. As you finalize your project, use these concepts as questions to self-check: can I show an isolated sensor test? Does my CSV continue to grow after a reboot? Can a subscriber receive my MQTT messages? These quick checks make your demo repeatable and robust.

When implementing alerts, protect GPIO with appropriate resistors and use relays or drivers for higher-power devices.
